title: Pilot‐scale photocatalytic treatment of textile wastewater using Cr–N–C–TiO2 nanocomposite: Effects of oxygenation patterns
content:
Abstract

This study explores the performance of a pilot scale photocatalytic oxidation (PCO) process that was designed to treat strong dye house effluent under different aeration patterns and reactor geometries. Photocatalysis was attained using an industrial-scale Cr–N–C–TiO2 thin film (TF) coated quartz sleeve containing 320 W-254 nm UV-C tube as irradiation source. As prepared TFs were characterized by X-ray diffraction (XRD), scanning electron microscopy (SEM), atomic force microscopy (AFM), X-ray photoelectron (XPS) and Raman spectroscopies. Two different reactor geometries (cylindrical & rectangular) and three aeration setups (air + perforated pipes (PP), air + fine bubble membrane diffusers (FBMD), pressurized pure oxygen (PPO) + FBMD) were experimented throughout the pilot study. Pseudo-first order COD and TKN decay rates ranged from 0.004 ± 0.0001 to 0.042 ± 0.001 min−1 and 0.001 ± 0.001 to 0.026 ± 0.001 min−1 depending on the altered experimental conditions. Although the highest oxygen transfer rates (SOTR and OTRf) were observed in a cylindrical reactor equipped with a vertical UV C tube position, the highest pollution reduction yields were obtained using the PPO + FBMD combination. COD and TKN removal efficiencies after 1 h of PCO through PPO-FBMD, air-FBMD and air-PP were 93 ± 5%, 46% ± 3, and 23% ± 3 and 77 ± 5%, 21 ± 3% and 13 ± 1% respectively. Effects of the reactor geometry and aeration patterns on oxygen reduction potential (ORP) parameter and pollutant removal efficiencies were also investigated systematically. Existing heavy metals and their removal/recovery pathways were studied as well. Energy usage figures of all aeration patterns were determined and compared with each other.
